candidates.quote: Some men say an army of horse and some men say an army on foot and some men say an army of ships is the most beautiful thing on the black earth. But I say it is what you love.
candidates.author: Sappho
candidates.locator: fragment 16, lines 1-4; If Not, Winter: Fragments of Sappho (Alfred A. Knopf, 2002)
candidates.whyThisMonth: An opening that lists what everyone else says and then, at the turn of the fourth line, decides for itself: a morning can start the same way.
candidates.year: c. 600 BCE (composed; the papyrus is 2nd century CE)

candidates.quote: Tell me about a complicated man.
candidates.author: Homer
candidates.locator: Book 1, line 1; The Odyssey (W. W. Norton, 2017)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The first line of the oldest journey story in the West asks for the whole of a person, complications included, before anything about him is proved.

candidates.quote: Although the wind blows terribly here, the moonlight also leaks between the roof planks of this ruined house.
candidates.author: Izumi Shikibu
candidates.locator: The Ink Dark Moon (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1988; Vintage Classics, 1990), Izumi Shikibu section, the poem beginning ‘Although the wind’
candidates.whyThisMonth: Light comes in through the same gaps the cold does, which is the thing to know about a January house and a January mood.

candidates.quote: Thence we came forth to rebehold the stars.
candidates.author: Dante Alighieri
candidates.locator: Canto XXXIV, line 139, the closing line; The Divine Comedy of Dante Alighieri (Ticknor and Fields, 1867)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The Inferno ends not in hell but on the way out of it, and the first thing seen on the far side is the sky before dawn.

candidates.quote: No coward soul is mine, no trembler in the world’s storm-troubled sphere: I see Heaven’s glories shine, and faith shines equal, arming me from fear.
candidates.author: Emily Brontë
candidates.locator: lines 1-4; first printed in Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey (Smith, Elder, 1850), Charlotte Brontë’s ‘Selections from the Literary Remains of Ellis Bell’
candidates.whyThisMonth: Dated the second of January in her manuscript, it is a year’s first declaration of nerve, made in the dark of the year.

candidates.quote: Ring out the old, ring in the new, ring, happy bells, across the snow: the year is going, let him go; ring out the false, ring in the true.
candidates.author: Alfred Tennyson
candidates.locator: section CVI (‘Ring out, wild bells’), lines 5-8; In Memoriam (Edward Moxon, 1850)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The New Year stanza the language reaches for by reflex, and all it asks is that the old year be let go.

candidates.quote: A word is dead when it is said, some say. I say it just begins to live that day.
candidates.author: Emily Dickinson
candidates.locator: Poems by Emily Dickinson, Third Series, ed. Mabel Loomis Todd (Roberts Brothers, 1896), Life VI
candidates.whyThisMonth: Six lines against the fear that saying a thing out loud ends it: on this reading the saying is where it starts.

candidates.author: Anton Chekhov
candidates.locator: Act IV, the last exchange before the family leaves (Trofimov, answering Anya’s ‘Good-bye to the old life!’); The Cherry Orchard and Other Plays (Chatto and Windus, 1923)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The last exchange of the play: the house is sold and shuttered, and the two youngest people in it walk out saying hello to what comes next.
candidates.speaker: Trofimov

candidates.quote: Rise, brothers, rise; the wakening skies pray to the morning light, the wind lies asleep in the arms of the dawn like a child that has cried all night.
candidates.author: Sarojini Naidu
candidates.whyThisMonth: A wake-up call written as a dawn: the sky is already praying for light and the wind is still asleep, so getting up is joining something under way.

candidates.author: Rainer Maria Rilke
candidates.work: Archaic Torso of Apollo (Archaïscher Torso Apollos)
candidates.locator: New Poems: The Other Part (1908), opening poem, line 14, the closing line; The Selected Poetry of Rainer Maria Rilke (Random House, 1982), p. 61
candidates.whyThisMonth: Five words at the end of a sonnet about a broken statue, and they are the most direct instruction in modern poetry.

candidates.quote: Nothing can ever happen twice. In consequence, the sorry fact is that we arrive here improvised and leave without the chance to practice.
candidates.author: Wisława Szymborska
candidates.locator: lines 1-4; first in Wołanie do Yeti (1957); View with a Grain of Sand: Selected Poems (Harcourt Brace, 1995)
candidates.whyThisMonth: No rehearsal and no repeat: the day that has never happened before is the only kind there is, which is a reason to get on with it.

candidates.quote: Yes, of course it hurts when buds are breaking. Why else would the springtime falter?
candidates.author: Karin Boye
candidates.work: Yes, Of Course It Hurts (Ja visst gör det ont)
candidates.locator: lines 1-2; För trädets skull (1935); Complete Poems (Bloodaxe Books, 1994)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Sweden’s best-known poem about beginning says the hard part is not failing but growing, and that the bud stayed shut all winter for a reason.

candidates.author: Samuel Beckett
candidates.locator: Act I, Winnie’s first words; Happy Days (Grove Press, 1961)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The opening line of the play: stuck fast and up to her waist in it, Winnie looks up and greets the day anyway, and the joke and the courage are the same thing.
candidates.speaker: Winnie

candidates.quote: Last year is dead, they seem to say, begin afresh, afresh, afresh.
candidates.author: Philip Larkin
candidates.locator: lines 10-12, the closing lines; High Windows (Faber and Faber, 1974)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The closing line of the plainest new-year poem in English: the trees are no younger than we are, they simply start again, and so can a reader.

candidates.quote: There is always something left to love. And if you ain’t learned that, you ain’t learned nothing.
candidates.author: Lorraine Hansberry
candidates.locator: Act III (Mama, to Beneatha); A Raisin in the Sun (Random House, 1959)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Said to a daughter ready to give up on her brother, on the morning the family moves house: the line for starting over with someone rather than without them.
candidates.speaker: Mama (Lena Younger)

candidates.quote: As you set out for Ithaka hope the voyage is a long one, full of adventure, full of discovery.
candidates.author: C. P. Cavafy
candidates.locator: lines 1-3; C. P. Cavafy: Collected Poems (Princeton University Press, 1975); the 1992 revised edition reads ‘hope your road is a long one’
candidates.whyThisMonth: The opening line is an instruction for setting out, and it asks not for a quick arrival but for a long, full way.
